title: What science knows about déjà vu: how common it is, what triggers it, and the memory explanation

Wait, Have I Been Here Before? The Curious Case of Déjà Vu

facts.text: Déjà vu is French for already seen.
A review of surveys estimated that about two-thirds of people have had déjà vu at least once.
A scene or place is the most common trigger of déjà vu, followed by a conversation.
Young people report déjà vu more often than older people, and it usually becomes less frequent with age.
Researchers explain déjà vu as a memory effect: a new scene that resembles a forgotten one, for example in its layout, produces a feeling of familiarity without recall of the source.
In experiments, people who felt during déjà vu that they knew what would happen next were no more accurate than chance.
In some people with epilepsy, déjà vu is linked to seizure activity in the medial temporal lobe of the brain.
